tier_reason: The README prints the full test_yuv_rgb output (std 2.630193 s, sse2_unaligned 0.704394 s, ffmpeg 1.221432/1.227100 s, ipp 0.636 s, sse2_aligned 0.606648 s; rgb2yuv sse2 0.640630/0.676625 s vs ffmpeg 3.385816/3.397952 s) with gcc 4.9.2, swscale 3.0.0, IPP 9.0.1 and an Intel i7-5500U; the timing harness is public (test_yuv_rgb.c, clock() over 100 iterations, sws_scale and ippiYCbCr420ToRGB_8u_P3C3R baselines) and the flags follow from the public CMakeLists.txt plus the documented Release build (CMake's GCC Release preset is -O3 -DNDEBUG).

corrections.caveats: Author's own run on one laptop CPU (i7-5500U) with an old swscale 3.0.0 whose YUV420P to RGB24 path is MMX code; modern swscale has newer SIMD paths and would narrow the gap. Intel IPP 9.0.1 beat the SSE2 code on rgb2yuv (0.579-0.594 s vs 0.641-0.677 s) and was within 5% on yuv2rgb. The swscale contexts are created with flags 0 (default scaler) and the outputs of each method are written to separate files but never compared, so equivalence is not checked. The rgb2yuv gap (about 5.3x) is likely partly different work: swscale has no unscaled fast path for RGB24 input (its special case is BGR24), so the ffmpeg row probably ran the generic scaler with filtered chroma and higher-precision intermediates, while yuv2rgb uses 8-bit fixed-point coefficients and a plain 2x2 box average for chroma. The yuv2rgb direction (about 2x) is closer to like-for-like (both use one chroma sample per 2x2 block). Flags are the CMake Release preset (-O3 -DNDEBUG) plus -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -std=c99 from CMakeLists.txt; SSE2 is the x86-64 baseline so no -msse flag is needed. Single 4K image run 100 times (cache-warm). README numbers predate the Feb 2022 commits, which include a fix to the plain C (std) rgb2yuv path, not the SSE2 path.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly and the harness code is public, so tier A stands. The rgb2yuv 5.3x likely compares against swscale's generic (filtered-chroma) path rather than an equivalent converter; the 2x yuv2rgb figure is the more like-for-like headline. Last commit 2022-02-15, 191 stars, BSD-3-Clause, not archived.

tier_reason: docs/BENCHMARKS.md shows the claimed tables (JPG 2.10 s vs libvips parallel 5.24 s vs imageflow 6.60 s; PNG 3.43/6.18/8.41 s; BMP 1.65/4.72 s; WEBP 14.03/23.52/15.69 s; RAM 271 MB vs 460 MB on JPG) on a MacBook Pro M2, but no benchmark script exists in the repo (scripts/ holds only build and release scripts, examples/ only basic_resize.cpp), no compiler or exact commands are given, and only the author ran it: first-party without reproducible methodology.

corrections.caveats: On the benchmarked Apple M2 (ARM) the default Mitchell filter is not what runs: src/resizer.cpp (unchanged since v1.0.0) routes any downscale with the Mitchell or triangle filter to the project's own NEON kernels in src/simd_resize.cpp, a plain 2-tap fixed-point bilinear for ratios under 3x (JPG 1179 to 800, PNG 2104 to 800, BMP 1045 to 800) and a box/area average above 3x (WEBP 4275 to 800); stb_image_resize2 is only the fallback (x86, upscaling, Catmull-Rom/box filters). So the measured path does less filtering than the requested Mitchell and than libvips' default kernel, and the 2-tap bilinear at 2.6x (PNG) aliases; the comparison is not quality-equivalent. Baseline libvips 8.15 was driven through the vips CLI ('parallel' row; how the parallelism and per-image processes were arranged is not stated) and imageflow 2.0 through imageflow_tool, so process start-up likely counts against the baselines. Benchmark commands and scripts are not published, one machine, two runs, no compiler or flags stated (CMakeLists.txt sets -O3, plus -march=native on x86). JPEG/PNG/WebP coding goes through libjpeg-turbo, libpng and libwebp, so much of the time is codec work. Repo is new (first commit 2025-12-03, latest 2026-01-07, 21 commits); 'fastest on the planet' is marketing language.

notes: Numbers match BENCHMARKS.md and README. The record's claim that the resize kernel is stb_image_resize2 is wrong for the benchmarked M2: downscales use the repo's own NEON bilinear/area code, which substitutes a cheaper filter for the default Mitchell; stb_image_resize2 is the x86/upscale fallback (relevant if the orchestrator considers a duplicate of stb). 67 stars, BSD-3-Clause, last commit 2026-01-07.

tier_reason: The README tables match the claim (Ryzen 7 3700X: 11919 vs 4899 ms at 1 thread, 2543 vs 822 ms at 8 threads; i7 10600U: 11719 vs 6010 ms at 1 thread). The benchmark code is public (Examples/H264SharpBenchmark/Program.cs, ConverterVersusOpenCV, against OpenCvSharp4 4.10.0.20241108), but the compiler and flags behind the measured native DLL are not stated (the benchmark folder ships a prebuilt H264SharpNative-win64.dll; repo build files offer ClangCL with AVX2 and a CMake -O3 -msse4.2 build), so first-party with partial methodology: C.

corrections.caveats: Benchmark code is in the repo (Examples/H264SharpBenchmark/Program.cs): each iteration times a YUV420 to RGB plus RGB to YUV420 round trip on a 1080p image for both libraries, called from C# (OpenCvSharp4 4.10.0.20241108, i.e. OpenCV 4.10, Windows runtime), with Cv2.SetNumThreads set to the same thread count as the converter's custom thread pool, so threading is matched. The committed config.json uses 1000 iterations and 1 thread, not the README's 5000, and the README does not say which build of the native DLL (prebuilt H264SharpNative-win64.dll in the benchmark folder) or which compiler and flags were used. Outputs are not compared: the converter uses 8-bit fixed-point BT.601 coefficients (Rgb2Yuv.cpp) and averages each 2x2 block for chroma, while OpenCV's cvtColor uses higher-precision fixed point, so results are not bit-identical. The 'up to 2.9x' headline matches the 4-thread Ryzen row (2.92x); the 8-thread row is about 3.1x, the 16-thread row 3.0x, the 1-thread row 2.4x and the Intel laptop rows 1.5-2.1x (derived from page data). Primary language is C#; the C++ converter (H264SharpNative/Rgb2Yuv*.cpp, Yuv2Rgb*.cpp with SSE, AVX2 and NEON variants) is one component of an OpenH264 wrapper. Last commit 2025-03-14.

notes: Numbers match the README; the record's caveat that benchmark code is absent was wrong (Examples/H264SharpBenchmark/Program.cs runs the OpenCV comparison with matched thread counts).
